paras: The Hunnewell Furnace Regulators attack was a night fight on March 20, 1881, at Brown-town, Greenup County, Kentucky, between a band of "Regulators" and Black ore-diggers whose hiring it opposed. One Black digger was wounded in the face and one Regulator was shot, the furnace was put under armed guard, and eight of the band were jailed. Papers carried it as part of a Regulator "reign of terror" around Grayson and in adjoining Greenup County.

Hunnewell Furnace stood four miles below Grayson on the Eastern Kentucky Railroad, where, according to the dispatch, "irresponsible ruffians" had tried to control the company's business. About the first of March, Superintendent Sebastian Gifort sent his son and clerk, Joseph Gifort, to Virginia, and the son returned with about forty Black ore-diggers. Their employment "incensed the so-called regulators," who sent anonymous notices telling both Giforts to leave the country or "suffer the penalty, death."

On the night of the 20th, about twelve or fifteen Regulators met a party of the diggers in Brown-town, and in what the report called "a brisk fight" several shots were fired. One of the Black men received a face wound, and a Regulator named Jones was shot through the groin. The diggers fell back to the furnace and asked for protection, and Gifort armed about two hundred employees to meet the band.

Armed men then guarded the furnace day and night, while the Regulators threatened death and the burning of the property. Eight members of the band were reported arrested and held in jail at Catlettsburg, but no report of a trial for the Hunnewell fight was found.

The episode is known from a single Grayson dispatch, printed in the Wheeling Register on March 31 under "Kentucky Regulators: Inaugurate a Reign of Terror in Certain Localities" and in the Lexington Kentucky Gazette on April 2 under "Rough Riders. Bad Work of Kentucky Regulators." Both condemned the band's "unlawful depredations," called the workers "negroes" and "black men," and ran the fight beside a Regulator whipping of the Bellamy family for "alleged immorality." The Gazette's subhead, "Furnace in a State of Siege," centered the company's defense of its property; the wounded digger was never named.

reader.title: Hunnewell Furnace Regulators attack
bases: An organized band calling itself 'Regulators' sent death notices over the hiring of about forty Black ore-diggers and then fought a party of the diggers at night, wounding one (A1, A2).

No one was killed: one Black digger was wounded in the face and a Regulator was shot in the groin (A1, A2). The band of twelve to fifteen acted without legal authority against the employment of Black workers, but the episode does not meet the killing requirement of the definition.
Both reports are prints of one Grayson dispatch with near-identical text (A1, A2); no independent or local account was found.

accounts.label: Grayson dispatch
accounts.gist: Regulators angered by the hiring of Black diggers sent death notices, then twelve to fifteen of them met a party of diggers at Brown-town; in a 'brisk fight' one digger and one Regulator were wounded, the furnace was put under armed guard, and eight Regulators were jailed.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Register headed it 'Kentucky Regulators: Inaugurate a Reign of Terror' and spoke of their 'unlawful depredations against the public'.
The Kentucky Gazette headed it 'Rough Riders. Bad Work of Kentucky Regulators' and called the band 'irresponsible ruffians' who forced the company to arm its employees.

conflicts.note: Same text; the dateline differs by a day. Both place the fight on the night of the 20th.
